$description: The reference input: an exact picture of the repository on the day the gate was written. It MUST pass — every case beside it is built on a copy of it, so a defective reference would turn all their „it fired" into falsehoods.

policy.$description: The browser matrix (req-quality-browsers). A second reading of what playwright.config.mts declares: that file configures, this one describes the CONTRACT, and tools/check-browsers.mjs asks Playwright what it really collected and requires all three to agree. Striking an engine out or widening an exclusion then takes two edits at once — that is, it leaves a sentence in the diff to read.
policy.$engines: Three engines, not three brands. `Desktop Edge` and `Google Chrome` are the same blink, so a fourth project would cost CI time and answer no new question. `baseline` marks the engine that runs WITH NO exclusions — the gate requires exactly one such and watches that nobody starts narrowing it.
policy.$exclusions: Every spec file runs on EVERY engine unless it stands here. `kind` says what justifies the entry: `record` is a decision somebody took and wrote down, `measurement` is a fact about the engine the gate repeats on every run (point 6) — so that an exclusion does not outlive the reason it was created for.

exclusions.reason: The baselines in `src/__screenshots__/linux/` came from a chromium rasterisation and every other engine differs from them because of the machine, not the code — measured: 26 of 26 baselines differ on firefox and just as many on webkit. A separate set of baselines per engine is three times the attention on every deliberate change of appearance and zero new questions: what the layout does on another engine is measured by the geometry tests, which run there in full. The promise of `req-quality-browsers` itself speaks of FUNCTIONAL tests and leaves screenshots on one platform.

Playwright's webkit reports `matchMedia('(forced-colors: active)').matches === true` and does not replace the author's colours: a probe with a `rgb(1, 2, 3)` background comes out of it unchanged, while chromium and firefox return a colour from the user's palette. `forced-color-adjust` is not even a known property there (`getComputedStyle` returns `undefined`). This whole file would ask about behaviour the engine does not have — and would ask QUIETLY: four of its six tests pass there, measuring colours from the tokens instead of from the palette. A real Safari does not enter this mode anyway: `forced-colors` is Windows High Contrast, and the macOS „Increase contrast" is `prefers-contrast`.
